title: Short Stuff: Why do kangaroos hop?
summary: Short Stuff episode on why and how kangaroos hop. Josh and Chuck cover kangaroos as marsupials, their history of European discovery (Francisco Pelsert sighting, arrival in London), the name's uncertain Aboriginal origin, and why kangaroos are the only large mammal that hops. They discuss fossil evidence that ancestors climbed in rainforests before hopping, the fourth toe and elastic tendons that store and release energy, top speeds and jump distances, tail counterbalance, respiratory efficiency during hopping, and differences between kangaroos and wallabies. The episode ends with off-topic recommendations of animated shows and the movie Enemy.

segments.title: Opening and credits to sources
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Short Stuff on kangaroo hopping and the hosts credit former colleagues' HowStuffWorks articles and other sources.

segments.title: Marsupials and the pouch
segments.summary: Chuck explains kangaroos are marsupials with a pouch where joeys develop. Josh describes marsupial birth and the joey latching onto a nipple that swells. They note the opossum episode and that kangaroos and wallabies have two legs and two small arms.

segments.title: European discovery and the name kangaroo
segments.summary: Chuck describes early European sightings, traced to Dutch merchant Francisco Pelsert shipwrecked off Australia in 1629, and kangaroos reaching London by 1791. Josh says the word kangaroo's origin is uncertain, possibly an Aboriginal phrase meaning roughly 'I don't know'.

segments.title: Only large mammals that hop
segments.summary: Chuck notes kangaroos are the only large mammals that move primarily by hopping. Fossil evidence suggests that about 25 million years ago, when Australia was rainforest, ancestors climbed rather than hopped.

segments.title: Foot anatomy and the fourth toe
segments.summary: Josh describes the kangaroo foot: a small or missing first toe, fused second and third toes, and a large fourth toe in line with the leg bones that enables hopping. Chuck notes this adaptation predates hopping and may have helped as they moved to dry grassy plains.

segments.title: Elastic tendons, speed and jump height
segments.summary: Chuck explains strong elastic tendons in the hind legs store energy on landing and release it in the jump. Josh gives top speeds of 15 to 20 miles per hour and jumps of about 25 feet forward and six feet high. The hosts joke about jumping over them.

segments.title: Height banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about their heights and shrinking with age, and Chuck suggests a future episode on shrinking.

segments.title: Tail as counterbalance
segments.summary: Chuck explains the large tail moves down during the jump and rises on landing, counterbalancing the hind feet. Josh says hopping is an efficient way to move quickly across land.

segments.title: Energy efficiency and breathing during hopping
segments.summary: Chuck says kangaroos are among the most efficient travelers in the animal kingdom, partly because the abdominal muscles move the respiratory system during hopping. Josh adds that less leg muscle is needed at speed and that the tail acts as a third foot when grazing slowly.

segments.title: Fifth leg aside
segments.summary: The hosts briefly question a line in the article that refers to a fifth leg, noting it conflicts with the two front arms described.

segments.title: Kangaroo vs wallaby
segments.summary: Chuck says kangaroos are much bigger, with more ankle-knee linkage and heights up to about eight feet, while wallabies are around three feet.

segments.title: Off-topic animated shows and the film Enemy
segments.summary: Hosts trade recommendations: Rocko's Modern Life (wallaby character), Darkwing Duck, Bluey, and the Jake Gyllenhaal film Enemy, including a discussion of its ending and online explanations.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh closes the episode and the standard iHeartRadio credit is read.
